q: A shop's file holds each customer's name, address and current balance. It is kept permanently and brought up to date from time to time. What type of file is it?
x: A master file holds the main, permanent data of a system, such as customers' balances, and is updated from time to time. A transaction file holds only recent changes, such as one day's sales.

q: Which of these is information rather than raw data?
o: The marks 67, 72 and 81 typed in from answer sheets
A list of roll numbers copied from the register
The scores read from quiz sheets before any working
The class average of 73 worked out from all the marks
x: Information is data that has been processed into a meaningful result, such as an average. Marks, scores or roll numbers as they are first typed in are raw data that has not been processed yet.

q: A direct file stores each record at the address given by key mod 9 (the remainder after dividing the key by 9). Keys 20 and 29 both give address 2. What is this situation called?
x: 20 mod 9 = 2 and 29 mod 9 = 2, so two different keys are sent to the same address; this is a collision, and one record must be placed elsewhere. Redundancy means the same data stored twice, which is not the case here.

q: A sequential file holds 600 records. Records are read one by one from the start until the wanted one is found. On average, about how many records are read to find a record that is in the file?
x: The wanted record is equally likely to be anywhere in the file, so on average about half the file, 600 ÷ 2 = 300 records, is read. Reaching a record in one read needs direct access, not sequential reading.

q: A file must use direct (random) organisation so that any record can be reached at once without reading the others. On which storage medium can it be kept?
o: A reel of punched paper tape
x: A disk's read/write head can move straight to any address, so direct files are kept on disks. Tape must be wound past every earlier record, so it allows sequential access only.

q: In a file-based system, the rule "marks cannot be more than 100" has to be written into every program that enters marks, and some programs forget it. Which limitation of file systems is this?
x: When each program must check rules such as marks ≤ 100 by itself, the rules are hard to enforce and change, so wrong data gets in; this is the integrity problem. Program-data dependence is about programs having to change when the record layout changes.

q: A sequential master file sorted by account number is updated in a single pass with one day's transactions. What must be done to the transaction file first?
o: Copy it onto a direct-access disk
Remove every account number that appears twice
x: In one pass the master file and the transaction file are read side by side, so both must be in the same key order or matching records would be missed. Date-and-time order is the order the transactions happened, and one account may rightly have several transactions.

q: A college replaces its separate Admissions, Library and Accounts files with one shared database in which each student's address is stored only once. What is the direct benefit?
o: Every office keeps its own copy of the address for safety
Programs must be rewritten whenever a field is added
A change of address is made once and every office sees the same address
Records can be read only in the order they were stored
x: Storing the address once removes redundancy, so one update keeps the data consistent for all offices. Keeping separate copies in each office is exactly the file-system problem the database removes.

q: An indexed sequential file has this index, each entry giving the lowest key in a block: 100 → block 1, 250 → block 2, 400 → block 3, 550 → block 4. Records are stored in key order. In which block is the record with key 390?
x: Block 2 holds the keys from 250 up to just below 400, and 250 ≤ 390 < 400, so the record is in block 2. Block 3 starts at key 400, which is already larger than 390.

q: A copy of the master file is kept on a separate disk so that the data can be restored if the original is damaged. What is this copy called?
x: A backup file is a copy kept for restoring data after loss or damage. A transaction file holds recent changes that are used to update the master file.

q: In which data model can a child record be linked to more than one parent record, so that the records form a graph-like structure?
x: The network model allows a record to have several parents, linked like a graph. The hierarchical model is a tree in which each child has exactly one parent.

q: A school database keeps the same table structure all year, but the rows in its tables change every day. What is the data stored in the database at one particular moment called?
x: An instance (state) is the actual data held at a given moment, and it changes as rows are added or edited. The schema is the structure, which stays the same.

q: In the relational model, what is a table formally called?
x: In relational terms a table is a relation, a row is a tuple and a column is an attribute. A domain is the set of allowed values of an attribute.

q: In Student(RollNo, Name, City), RollNo is unique, but two students may have the same Name and City. Which set of columns is a super key but NOT a candidate key?
x: {RollNo, Name} identifies every row because it contains RollNo, so it is a super key; it is not minimal, since RollNo alone already works, so it is not a candidate key. {RollNo} is a candidate key, and {Name, City} is not unique.

q: In Student(RollNo, Name, City), records are often searched and sorted by City, which is not unique. What kind of key is City?
x: A secondary key is a field used to search or sort records that need not be unique. Candidate and alternate keys must be unique, and City is not.

q: In Book(AccessionNo, ISBN, Title, Author), every physical copy has its own AccessionNo, and the library keeps several copies of many titles, which share one ISBN. Which column can be the primary key?
x: Only AccessionNo is different for every copy, so it can identify each row. ISBN is repeated for copies of the same title, so it is not unique in this table.

q: A DBMS keeps the names, data types and sizes of all fields and the tables they belong to, that is, data about the data. Where is this kept?
x: The data dictionary (catalogue) stores metadata, the description of the database's structure. A transaction file holds recent changes to data, not descriptions of the fields.

q: In the three-level architecture of a DBMS, which level describes how the data is actually stored on disk?
x: The internal level describes storage details such as files and indexes. The conceptual level describes the whole database's tables and relationships, and the external level the views seen by users.

q: A clerk enters data through ready-made forms and menus and never writes SQL or programs. What kind of database user is the clerk?
x: End users work with the database through forms, menus and reports made for them. Application programmers write those programs, and the DBA manages security, backup and performance.

q: Which statement about a table (relation) in the relational model is correct?
o: No two rows are exactly the same
Rows must be stored in primary-key order
One column may hold values of different types
Two columns may have the same name
x: Each row of a relation is unique, which the primary key guarantees. The order of rows does not matter, every column takes values from one domain, and column names in a table are different.

q: Department(DeptID, DName) and Teacher(TeacherID, TName, DeptID), where Teacher.DeptID is a foreign key to Department. Which statement is true?
o: Every DeptID in Teacher must be different
The same DeptID may appear in many Teacher rows
DeptID must be the primary key of Teacher
A DeptID in Teacher may be one that is not in Department
x: Many teachers can belong to one department, so a foreign key value may repeat on the many side. With referential integrity it must match a DeptID that exists in Department, and it is not Teacher's primary key.

q: Tables, primary key first: Student(RollNo, SName), Dept(DeptID, DName), Course(CourseID, Title, DeptID), Teacher(TeacherID, TName, DeptID), Enrol(RollNo, CourseID, Grade) with key (RollNo, CourseID). A column with the same name as another table's primary key is a foreign key to it. How many foreign key columns are there in all?
x: Course.DeptID, Teacher.DeptID, Enrol.RollNo and Enrol.CourseID refer to other tables: 4 columns. The two columns of Enrol's key are also foreign keys; missing them gives 2, and Student.RollNo is a primary key, not a foreign key.

q: Which DBMS feature stops a user who has no permission from viewing the staff salary table?
o: Security through user accounts and permissions
x: A DBMS controls access with user accounts, passwords and permissions, so only authorised users can see sensitive tables. Referential integrity is about foreign keys matching primary keys, not about who may read data.

q: In which data model are the data and the procedures that act on the data stored together as objects?
x: The object-oriented model stores objects that combine attributes (data) and methods (procedures). The relational model stores data only, in tables.

q: Two booking clerks try to sell the last seat on a bus at the same moment. Which DBMS function makes sure the seat is sold only once?
x: Concurrency control manages users who change the same data at the same time, so one sale finishes before the other can use the seat. Normalisation is a design method and does not control simultaneous users.

q: In database design, what is an entity?
o: A person, place, thing or event about which data is stored
A single value stored in one field of a record
A line that joins two shapes in a diagram
A rule that limits the values of a field
x: An entity is something of interest to the organisation, such as Student or Book, about which data is kept. A single stored value is an attribute's value, and a rule on values is a constraint.

q: Each country has exactly one capital city, and each capital city is the capital of one country. What type of relationship is Country–Capital?
x: One instance on each side is linked to exactly one instance on the other side, so the relationship is one-to-one. One-to-many would need a country with several capitals.

q: A student may have several phone numbers, and all of them are stored under the attribute Phone. What kind of attribute is Phone?
x: An attribute that can hold more than one value for one entity is multivalued (a double oval in an ER diagram). A composite attribute is split into parts, such as Address into Street and City.

q: In a company database, Dependent (an employee's child or spouse) cannot be identified by its own attributes; it is identified only together with the employee it belongs to. What is Dependent called?
x: An entity that has no key of its own and depends on another (owner) entity for identification is a weak entity, drawn as a double rectangle. A strong entity has its own key.

q: In the database life cycle, at which step is the ER diagram turned into tables with columns, primary keys and foreign keys for a relational DBMS?
x: Logical design maps the ER model to relations (tables) of the chosen data model. Conceptual design draws the ER diagram itself, and physical design decides storage and indexes.

q: Which order of database design steps is correct?
o: Physical design → logical design → conceptual design
Logical design → conceptual design → physical design
Conceptual design → physical design → logical design
Conceptual design → logical design → physical design
x: Design moves from the DBMS-independent ER model (conceptual), to tables (logical), to storage details on the chosen DBMS (physical). Storage cannot be planned before the tables are known.

q: Which pair is in a many-to-many relationship?
o: Person and CNIC: each person has one CNIC and each CNIC belongs to one person
Book and Author: a book can have several authors and an author can write several books
Team and Player: a team has many players and each player plays for one team
Mother and Child: a mother can have many children and each child has one mother
x: Only Book–Author has "many" on both sides. Team–Player and Mother–Child are one-to-many, and Person–CNIC is one-to-one.

q: A hospital's rules: each doctor works in one department, and a department has many doctors; a doctor treats many patients, and a patient can be treated by many doctors. Which description of the relationships is correct?
x: A department has many doctors but each doctor has one department, so that is one-to-many. Doctors and patients are "many" on both sides, so that is many-to-many.

q: Employee(EmpID, Name, ManagerID) stores in ManagerID the EmpID of each employee's manager, who is also an employee. What does ManagerID refer to?
o: The primary key EmpID of the same Employee table
The primary key of a separate Manager table that must be created
Nothing, since a table cannot refer to itself
A composite key made of EmpID and Name
x: This is a unary (recursive) relationship, so ManagerID is a foreign key that points to EmpID in the same table. No separate Manager table is needed, because managers are employees too.

q: A school database has been in use for two years. The users now need a field for each student's blood group, and it is added to the working system. Which stage of the database life cycle is this?
x: Changes made to a database that is already in operation, to meet new needs or fix problems, belong to the maintenance stage. The design stages come before the database is first built.

q: Teaches(TeacherID, SubjectID) has the rows (T1, S1), (T1, S2), (T2, S1), (T3, S3). Which relationship between Teacher and Subject do these rows show?
x: T1 teaches two subjects (S1 and S2), and S1 is taught by two teachers (T1 and T2), so both sides are "many". One-to-many from Teacher would need each subject to have only one teacher, which S1 breaks.

q: What is the main aim of normalisation?
o: To give every table as many columns as possible
To store the same data in several tables for safety
To sort every table by its primary key
To reduce redundancy and avoid insertion, update and deletion anomalies
x: Normalisation splits tables so that each fact is stored once, which removes the anomalies caused by repeated data. Storing data in several places is the redundancy it tries to remove.

q: In the functional dependency RollNo → Name, what is RollNo called?
x: The attribute on the left of the arrow determines the one on the right, so RollNo is the determinant and Name is the dependent attribute.

q: Staff(StaffID, Name, Dept, DeptPhone) repeats the department's phone number in every staff row. The Sales department has 6 staff. Its phone number changes. How many rows must be changed to keep the table correct?
x: The number is stored once for each of the 6 Sales staff, so all 6 rows must be changed; changing fewer leaves an update anomaly. In a normalised design it would be stored once in a Department table.

q: In Book(BookID, PublisherID, PublisherCity), BookID → PublisherID and PublisherID → PublisherCity, and PublisherID is not a key. What kind of dependency does PublisherCity have on BookID?
x: PublisherCity depends on BookID only through the non-key attribute PublisherID, which is a transitive dependency, the problem 3NF removes. A partial dependency needs a composite key, and BookID is a single column.

q: Marks(Roll, Subject, Name, Score) has the key (Roll, Subject), with Roll → Name and (Roll, Subject) → Score. Which non-key attribute is fully functionally dependent on the whole key?
x: Score needs both Roll and Subject to be known, so it depends on the whole key. Name depends on Roll alone, which is a partial dependency.

q: A relation has the functional dependencies P → Q and Q → S. Which dependency must also hold?
x: If each P value fixes one Q value, and each Q value fixes one S value, then each P value fixes one S value, so P → S (transitivity). The reverse directions are not implied.

q: Emp(EmpID, Name, DeptID, DeptHead) has the key EmpID, with EmpID → Name, EmpID → DeptID and DeptID → DeptHead. Which split puts it into 3NF without losing any information?
o: Emp(EmpID, Name, DeptHead) and Dept(DeptID, DeptHead)
Emp(EmpID, Name, DeptID) and Dept(DeptID, DeptHead)
x: The transitive part DeptID → DeptHead moves to its own table, and DeptID stays in Emp as a foreign key to link the two. Without DeptID in Emp there is no way to know which department an employee is in.

q: A table is in 1NF and its primary key is a single column. Which higher normal form is it then certain to be in?
x: A partial dependency means depending on part of a composite key, and a one-column key has no parts, so the table is in 2NF. It may still have a transitive dependency, so 3NF is not certain.

q: Order(OrderNo, Date, CustID, CustName, ProductID, ProductName, Qty) has the key (OrderNo, ProductID), with OrderNo → Date, OrderNo → CustID, CustID → CustName, ProductID → ProductName and (OrderNo, ProductID) → Qty. How many tables result when it is normalised to 3NF in the usual way?
x: The tables are OrderHead(OrderNo, Date, CustID), Customer(CustID, CustName), Product(ProductID, ProductName) and OrderLine(OrderNo, ProductID, Qty): 4. Stopping at 2NF would leave CustName with the order data and give 3.

q: Emp(EmpID, Name, DeptID, DeptName) is split into Emp(EmpID, Name, DeptID) and Dept(DeptID, DeptName). Which of these becomes possible?
o: Recording a new department before any employee joins it
Storing the department name in every employee row
Giving two departments the same DeptID
Deleting a department that still has employees without any check
x: A department can now be a row of Dept on its own, so the insertion anomaly is gone. Storing the name in every employee row is the redundancy the split removed.

q: After normalisation, Student(Roll, Name, ClassID) and Class(ClassID, Teacher) were made from one table. How can each student's name be shown with the class teacher?
o: Join the two tables on Name and Teacher
Join the two tables on the common column ClassID
Copy Teacher back into every Student row
Add Roll to Class as a second key
x: The foreign key ClassID in Student matches the primary key of Class, so joining on it brings each student's row together with the class's teacher. Copying Teacher back would bring the redundancy back.

q: Teacher(TeacherID, Name, DeptID) has DeptID as a foreign key to Dept, with referential integrity enforced. DeptID is not set as required. A new teacher is added with DeptID left empty (NULL) because the department is not decided yet. What happens?
o: It is refused, because a foreign key can never be NULL
It is refused, because it breaks entity integrity
It is allowed only if DeptID is the primary key of Teacher
It is allowed, because a foreign key may be NULL unless it is made required
x: Referential integrity says a non-empty foreign key must match a primary key value; an empty (NULL) value matches nothing and is allowed unless the field is required. Entity integrity applies to the primary key TeacherID, not to DeptID.
